'''''Ceropegia''''' is a [[genus]] of plants within the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Apocynaceae]], native to Africa, southern Asia, and Australia.<ref>Bruyns, P. V. & P. I. Forster. 1991. Recircumscription of the Stapelieae (Asclepiadaceae). Taxon 40(3): 381–391</ref><ref name=foc>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=106259 Flora of China Vol. 16 Page 266 <big>吊灯花属</big> diao deng hua shu ''Ceropegia'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 211. 1753. ]</ref>  It was named by [[Carl Linnaeus]], who first described this genus in his ''Genera plantarum'', which appeared in 1737.<ref name="Gen Plant">{{cite book |last1=Linnaei |first1=Caroli |title=Genera plantarum... |date=1737 |publisher=Conradum Wishoff |location=Leiden |page=65 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/43565185#page/87/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> Linnaeus referred to the description and picture of a plant in the ''Horti Malabarici'' as the plant for which the genus was created.<ref name="Hort Mal">{{cite book |last1=Rhede (or Reede) tot Drakestein |first1=Hendrik |title=Horti Malabarici Pars Nona |date=1689 |volume=9 |location=Amsterdam |pages=27–28 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/14379#page/45/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> In 1753 he named this species as ''[[Ceropegia candelabrum]]''.<ref name="Spec Plant">{{cite book |last1=Linnaei |first1=Caroli |title=Species plantarum... Tomus I |date=1753 |publisher=Laurentii Salvii |location=Stockholm |page=211 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84235#page/225/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> Linnaeus did not explain the etymology but later explanations stated that the name ''Ceropegia'' was from the Greek<ref name="The Ling Grae">{{cite book |last1=Stephano |first1=Henr. |title=Thesauri linguæ Græcæ Tomus II |date=1572 |publisher=Henrico Stephano |page=193 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=ucm.5316860352&view=1up&seq=109 |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> word ''keropegion'' κηροπηγɩον.<ref name="All Poly">{{cite book |last1=Nemnich |first1=Philipp Andreas |title=Allgemeines Polyglotten-Lexicon der Naturgeschichte mit erklaerenden Anmerkungen |date=1793 |volume=1 |publisher=Licentiat Nemnich |location=Hamburg |page=954 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/73587#page/499/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref><ref name="Enc Lond">{{cite book |last1=Wilkes |first1=John |title=Encyclopædia Londinensis Vol. IV |date=1810 |publisher=J. Adlard |location=London |page=42 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/265417#page/58/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> This means ''candelabrum'' in Latin, which has a broader range than the modern word - "a candlestick, a branched candlestick, a chandelier, candelabrum, or also lamp-stand, light-stand, sometimes of exquisite workmanship".<ref name="Lat Dicti">{{cite web |last1=Lewis |first1=Charlton T |last2=Short |first2=Charles |title=A Latin Dictionary |url=http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0059%3Aentry%3Dcandelabrum |website=Perseus Digital Library |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref>

An alternative explanation for the name was given later by William Jackson Hooker in 1830 in ''Curtis's Botanical Magazine'' in the description of ''[[Ceropegia elegans]]'': "From ''[[wikt:κηρός#Ancient Greek|κηρός]]'', wax, and ''[[wikt:πηγή#Ancient Greek|πηγή]]'', a fountain, in allusion to the delicate, waxy umbels of some species".<ref name="Hook Beaut">{{cite journal |last1=Hooker |first1=William Jackson |title=Ceropegia elegans. Beautiful Ceropegia. |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |date=1830 |volume=57 |page=Folio 3015 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/495035#page/186/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> However, four years later Hooker gave the etymology in the description in the same periodical of ''[[Ceropegia bulbosa|Ceropegia lushii]]'' as "remarkable for the peculiar shape of its flowers, frequently arranged in umbels, hence its name κηροπηγɩον, a candelabrum, or lamp-stand".<ref name="Hook Lush">{{cite journal |last1=Hooker |first1=William Jackson |title=Ceropegia Lushii. Mr. Lush's Ceropegia. |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |date=1834 |volume=61 |page=Folio 3300 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/14340#page/35/mode/1up |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref>

They have many common names including lantern flower, parasol flower, parachute flower, bushman's pipe, string of hearts, snake creeper, wine-glass vine, rosary vine, and necklace vine.

''Ceropegia'' species are traded, kept, and propagated as [[ornamental plant]]s.<ref name="ollerton">Ollerton, J., Masinde, S., Meve, U., Picker, M., & Whittington, A. (2009). [[doi:10.1093/aob/mcp072|Fly pollination in ''Ceropegia'' (Apocynaceae: Asclepiadoideae): biogeographic and phylogenetic perspectives.]] {{cbignore|bot=medic}} ''Annals of Botany'', mcp072.</ref> In Africa, the roots and leaves of some species are eaten raw<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pieroni |first1=Andrea |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=30 |isbn=0415927463 }}</ref> and the tubers in India are eaten raw or stewed in curries.<ref name="Hook Lush" />

==Appearance==
[[File:Ceropegia linearis subsp woodii.jpg|thumb|right|130px|''[[Ceropegia woodii]]'']]

The stems are vining or trailing in most species, though a few species from the Canary Islands have erect growth habits. Among some species, such as ''[[Ceropegia woodii]]'', the nodes swell, and the roots similarly expand to form tubers beneath the soil surface. The [[leaf|leaves]] are simple and opposite, although they can be rudimentary or absent. Especially in certain succulent species, the leaves may also be thick and fleshy.

The [[flower]]s have a tubular [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]] with five [[petal]]s most often fused at the tips, forming an umbrella-like canopy, a cage, or appendage-like antennae.<ref>Dyer, R.A. 1983. ''Ceropegia'', ''Brachystelma'' and ''Riocreuxia'' in Southern Africa. A.A. Balkema, Rotterdam.</ref> Pollination is accomplished by [[fly|flies]], and species can be generalists by attracting multiple families, or extremely specialized.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Coombs |first1=Gareth |last2=Dold |first2=Anthony P. |last3=Peter |first3=Craig I. |date=June 2011 |title=Generalized fly-pollination in Ceropegia ampliata (Apocynaceae–Asclepiadoideae): the role of trapping hairs in pollen export and receipt |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00606-011-0483-6 |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |language=en |volume=296 |issue=1–2 |pages=137–148 |doi=10.1007/s00606-011-0483-6 |bibcode=2011PSyEv.296..137C |s2cid=36698383 |issn=0378-2697 |via=Springer |url-access=subscription }}</ref> ''[[Ceropegia dolichophylla]]'' releases scents that attract [[Kleptoparasitism|kleptoparasitic]] flies by mimicking the pheromones released by predatory arthropods in distress.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heiduk |first1=A. |last2=Brake |first2=I. |last3=Tolasch |first3=T. |last4=Frank |first4=J. |last5=Jürgens |first5=A. |last6=Meve |first6=U. |last7=Dötterl |first7=S. |date=1 October 2010 |title=Scent chemistry and pollinator attraction in the deceptive trap flowers of Ceropegia dolichophylla |journal=South African Journal of Botany |series=Chemical diversity and biological functions of plant volatiles |language=en |volume=76 |issue=4 |pages=762–769 |doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2010.07.022 |issn=0254-6299 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2010SAJB...76..762H }}</ref> The flowers are often inflated and fused at several points, forming a cage. Flies become momentarily trapped inside, accomplishing pollination as they move about.<ref name=ollerton/>

==Classification==
The genus ''Ceropegia'' belongs to the subfamily [[Asclepiadoideae]] (milkweeds) within the family Apocynaceae. Species of this genus bear similarities to the carrion flowers or [[stapelia]]s. There are at least 420 known species.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |last1=Govaerts |first1=Rafaël |title=Ceropegia L. |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:328162-2 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=17 July 2021 }}</ref> More are being discovered and described regularly.<ref name=ollerton/><ref>[[Herbert Huber (botanist)|Herbert F. J. Huber]]: Revision of the genus Ceropegia. In: Memórias da Sociedade Broteriana, Volume 12, 1957, S.1-203, Coimbra</ref> They are distributed throughout most of sub-Saharan Africa and [[Madagascar]] to the Arabian Peninsula, southeast Asia, the Canary Islands, the tropical Pacific, and Australia.<ref name=ollerton/>

A generic complex, with many interesting [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] problems at both generic and specific level, is formed by three genera: ''Ceropegia'', ''[[Brachystelma]]'' and ''[[Riocreuxia]]''.
